title: The Misls
hook: twelve Sikh confederacies rule parts of Punjab in the late 1700s

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vadda Ghallughara, and your line, the panth rose again. Did you honor something that came back from hard times? Today, what the panth rose into. Day two hundred ninety-two.

A big extended family can work like a small federation. Every household runs its own home, its own budget, its own arguments. Cousins compete. Uncles don't always speak. But when there's a wedding, or a funeral, or someone's in trouble, everyone shows up, and for a day they're one family. In the late 1700s, Punjab was run a little like that. After decades of being hunted, the Sikhs now held the land, not as one kingdom, but as twelve. Today: the misls.
screen: `MANY HOUSEHOLDS, ONE FAMILY.` → `EVERYONE SHOWS UP.` → `PUNJAB IN THE 1700S: TWELVE.`

segments.voice: A misl was a Sikh confederacy: a band of fighters and their families under a leader, a sardar, holding its own territory. By the second half of the 1700s, as Afghan and Mughal power in Punjab faded, there were twelve main misls. They had names, some from a leader's village, some from a trait. The Bhangis, who at one time held Lahore and Amritsar. The Ahluwalias, led by Jassa Singh, the commander we met with the Dal Khalsa. The Ramgarhias, the Kanhaiyas, the Sukerchakias, and others. Each ran its own affairs. And they did not always get along. Misls competed, feuded, and sometimes fought each other. Historians don't hide that. Where the word misl comes from, sources differ. It's an Arabic word. Some explain it as alike or equal, because the misls were meant to be equals. Others as a file or record, because the bands were listed in one register. Both fit. Here's the part that makes the misls more than a set of rival chiefdoms. Twice a year, at Vaisakhi and Diwali, they still came to Amritsar as the Sarbat Khalsa, sat before the Guru Granth Sahib, and could pass a gurmata together. Faced with an outside threat, the twelve could move as one Dal Khalsa. Many also offered rakhi, protection, to villages in return for a share of the harvest. It was untidy, and it lasted only a few decades. But it held the Sikhs together through a dangerous time, and one of those twelve would soon produce a young leader who'd unite most of them.
screen: `MISL — A SIKH CONFEDERACY.` · `TWELVE, EACH WITH ITS OWN SARDAR.` · `RIVALS, WHO SOMETIMES FEUDED.` · `ONE BEFORE THE GURU, TWICE A YEAR.` · then, large: `TWELVE, AND ONE.`

segments.voice: Think of a group you belong to: your family, a team, friends, a congregation, a class. Picture the people in it, all different, some of whom don't quite get along. Now ask: what holds us together anyway? A shared meal, a shared story, something we all care about more than our quarrels? Name that one thing. Notice it, and let yourself be grateful for it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Misl. One of the twelve Sikh confederacies that ruled parts of Punjab in the late 1700s: separate, often rival, and one before the Guru.
Your line: twelve, and one. Today, in a group that argues, point once to the thing you all share. Day two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Some Sikh families still trace their history to one of the twelve misls; the misl period is taught in Sikh history as the bridge between the persecution of the early 1700s and the kingdom of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

original.note: Gurmukhi spelling of an Arabic word, explained as alike or equal, or as a file or record.

trapdoor: what it means: twelve Sikh confederacies, separate and sometimes rival, that still came together before the Guru.
what a scholar hears: the misl period runs roughly from the 1760s to Ranjit Singh's unification around 1799–1801; the count of twelve sometimes includes the Phulkian misl and sometimes not.

sources.ref: The twelve misls of the late eighteenth century, as recorded in Sikh history

notes: The list of twelve varies (Phulkian sometimes counted, sometimes not); only five are named.
Etymology of misl (Arabic mithl 'alike' vs. 'file/record') given as competing explanations; confirm.
Duration 'about half a century' is approximate.

Review (fresh editor): hook no longer opens 'Think of'; 'about half a century' (roughly 1760s to 1799) softened; Ranjit Singh did not unite all twelve (the Phulkian states stayed outside), so 'all' became 'most'; 'many Sikh families' softened.
